novelty.justification: The idea's core method is described as 'a three-stage causal protocol that turns an observed macroscopic base-image energy gap into a specific, regime-annotated software root cause.' Closest entries such as R29 investigate base-image energy effects but lack root-cause/regime attribution; R27 attributes energy to code locations but not to libc×memory-regime causes. The contribution is a meaningful extension over prior macro/measurement/hotspot work rather than a new paradigm or merely swapping one module.
novelty.rubric: Incremental: a meaningful extension or optimization of prior baseline work that fixes a concrete prior limitation, but the core paradigm is unchanged.
novelty.differentiation: The Solution Space contains macro base-image energy-impact work (R29), energy measurement infrastructure (R24/R12), code-level energy profiling (R27), and glibc/musl memcpy source material (R11/R15), but none combine statistical macro-gap confirmation, trace-to-energy hotspot localization, and libc×regime microbenchmark isolation into a causal attribution table. EnergyDelta adds regime-dependence: musl memcpy is 'energy-vampiric only in the small-buffer / cache-resident regime' while streamed regimes are equivalent.

feasibility.justification: The plan explicitly relies on existing artifact data and tooling: 'all CPU-only, all from the mounted artifact,' 'the above are one script (project/experiment_runner.py); no GPU, no queue needed,' and 'No new bare-metal measurement was performed.' The main engineering burden is scripting CSV/uftrace processing and statistical analysis, not building new low-level infrastructure.
feasibility.rubric: Low barrier / easy to implement: core logic can be quickly built on existing Python libraries or common ML frameworks; only small changes to a standard evaluation flow (e.g. prompt strategy tweaks or swapping metrics).

clarity.justification: The proposal gives concrete steps and metrics: 'Redis energy stats (7 configs × 30 runs) with block-bootstrap CI + Welch + Mann-Whitney + Cohen's d,' plus memcpy microbenchmark and causal reconciliation. It also includes 'Provenance & threats to validity' and reviewer objections with responses. It is detailed enough to become a solid proposal, though the causal mixture model and trace/energy alignment are described conceptually rather than at pseudocode or equation level.
clarity.rubric: Clear and concrete: steps are explicit with a reasonable, specific experiment design (baseline tools, metric definitions); can be turned into a solid proposal.

claims.statement: The proposed energy debugging methodology helps identify and isolate energy consumption hotspots in software systems and their dependencies.
claims.evidence_quote: This paper presents an energy debugging methodology for identifying and isolating energy consumption hotspots in software systems.

claims.statement: Redis packaged for Alpine consumes about 14.5% more energy than Redis packaged for Ubuntu while taking roughly the same time.
claims.evidence_quote: The Alpine version uses around 14.5 % more energy than the Ubuntu version while taking roughly the same time to complete.

claims.statement: After using the same recent Redis version, the Alpine/musl image still uses around 10% more energy than Ubuntu, so Redis version differences are not the only explanation.
claims.evidence_quote: However, there is still a significant gap between Alpine and Ubuntu, with Alpine using around 10 % more energy than Ubuntu.

claims.statement: When configurations are equal except for libc, Alpine/musl consumes 8.6% more total energy and up to 20.2% more CPU power than Ubuntu/glibc for the Redis benchmark.
claims.evidence_quote: we observe a difference of 8.6 % in total energy consumption and up to 20.2 % in power usage.

claims.statement: Alpine with glibc performs similarly to Ubuntu and considerably better than Alpine with musl, indicating the libc implementation is the primary cause.
claims.evidence_quote: the image performs considerably better than any of the Alpine images with musl.

claims.statement: In traced Redis execution, memcpy dominates libc activity, representing 39.6% of traced runtime and 92.6% of calls.
In a cache-to-memory memcpy benchmark that mimics Redis small copies, musl is about 15.8% more power hungry and takes almost 3x longer than glibc, causing much higher total energy consumption.
claims.evidence_quote: musl is much more power hungry than glibc, with a difference of around 1.1W or 15.8 % difference ... Alpine taking almost 3× more time

claims.statement: In a large 12 GB memcpy benchmark, Alpine/musl uses slightly more power but finishes faster and consumes slightly less total energy than Ubuntu/glibc, showing workload-dependent behavior.
claims.evidence_quote: Alpine image ends up taking slightly less overall energy to complete the task.

claims.statement: The observed difference is attributed to memcpy implementations: glibc has additional assembly-level optimization while musl implements memcpy in C.
claims.evidence_quote: glibc seems to have additional optimization with some assembly code, while musl does not.

original.overall_conclusion: The paper presents a methodology for debugging software energy consumption and demonstrates it on Redis. It finds that Redis on Alpine consumes more energy than on Ubuntu, with up to 20.2% higher CPU power in certain operations, and traces the cause to the musl implementation of memcpy. Custom benchmarks confirm workload-dependent energy differences between musl and glibc.
original.comparable_notes: Experiments used EnergiBridge on an AMD Ryzen 9 7900X with fixed CPU frequency/voltage, single-core isolation, 30 randomized executions, CPU warm-up via Sysbench, Redis redis-benchmark workload, and Docker images with controlled Redis version, compiler/libc, and allocator configurations. Small-copy memcpy behavior depends on compiler-visible information, so benchmark design matters.

agent.overall_conclusion: EnergyDelta localizes Docker base-image energy regressions: Alpine/musl consumes 12.7% more energy than Ubuntu/glibc for Redis and 13.2% more for PostgreSQL, driven by libc rather than the distribution image, with musl memcpy being energy-expensive mainly in the cache-resident regime and accounting for about 40% of attributable Redis runtime.
